chapterTitle: If Christ Has Not Been Raised — The Resurrection, the Last Enemy and the Victory

scripture.text: Now I declare to you, brothers, the Good News which I preached to you, which also you received, in which you also stand,
scripture.understanding: Paul now addresses the deepest problem in Corinth: some were denying the resurrection of the dead (v. 12). He begins not with an argument but with a reminder: γνωρίζω — I make known again — the εὐαγγέλιον I preached, which you παραλαμβάνω — received — and in which you ἵστημι, stand. The gospel is not something you graduate from. It is the ground under your feet.

scripture.text: by which also you are saved, if you hold firmly the word which I preached to you—unless you believed in vain.
scripture.understanding: By this gospel you are being σῴζω — saved; the present tense: it is still saving you — if you κατέχω, hold firmly, to the word as Paul preached it. “Unless you believed εἰκῇ — in vain, without effect.” Paul is not doubting their salvation; he is warning that a faith which lets go of the resurrection was never holding the real gospel.

scripture.text: For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures,
scripture.understanding: Ἐν πρώτοις — as of first importance. Paul παραδίδωμι — handed on — what he himself παραλαμβάνω — received: the technical words for transmitting sacred tradition, as in 11:23. What follows in verses 3 to 5 has the rhythm of an early creed, which many scholars across the theological spectrum date to within a few years of the crucifixion. First article: Christ ἀπέθανεν — died — ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν — for our sins — “according to the γραφαί, the Scriptures” (Isaiah 53).

scripture.text: that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,
scripture.understanding: Second article: ἐτάφη — He was buried. The burial confirms the reality of the death — a real body in a real tomb. Third article: ἐγήγερται — He has been raised. The verb is perfect tense: He was raised and remains risen. “On the third day according to the Scriptures” (compare Hosea 6:2; Jonah 1:17, which Jesus Himself applied to His resurrection in Matthew 12:40).

scripture.text: and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.
scripture.understanding: Fourth article: ὤφθη — He appeared, He was seen. First to Κηφᾶς — Peter, using his Aramaic name (compare Luke 24:34, “The Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!”). Then to the Twelve — the title for the apostolic group, even though Judas was gone. This list is legal testimony. The women, who were the first witnesses according to all four Gospels, are not named here — very possibly because the list follows the form of formal public testimony, in which a woman's witness was given little weight in that culture.

scripture.text: Then he appeared to over five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, but some have also fallen asleep.
scripture.understanding: Then ἐπάνω πεντακοσίοις — to more than five hundred brothers ἐφάπαξ — at one time. Not a private vision or a single excited group; a crowd. And Paul adds a challenge: “most of whom remain until now.” In other words: they are alive; go and ask them. Some have κοιμάω — fallen asleep — the Christian word for death, because death is no longer final.

scripture.text: Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles,
scripture.understanding: Then to Ἰάκωβος — James, the Lord's brother, who had not believed in Jesus during His ministry (John 7:5) and became a leader of the Jerusalem church (Galatians 1:19; Acts 15). What changes a sceptical brother into a man who will die for his brother's claims? An appearance of the risen Christ. Then to all the apostles.

scripture.text: and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also.
scripture.understanding: Last of all, to Paul — ὡσπερεὶ τῷ ἐκτρώματι, “as to one untimely born.” Ἔκτρωμα means a miscarriage, a stillborn or abnormally born child. It may have been an insult Paul's opponents used of him — an apostle born wrong — which he humbly accepts. He saw the risen Christ on the Damascus road, after the others, out of season.

words.english: child born at the wrong time

scripture.text: For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God.
scripture.understanding: Ἐλάχιστος — the least. Paul calls himself the least of the apostles, not ἱκανός — not fit, not sufficient — to be called an apostle, because he διώκω — persecuted — the church of God. He never forgot it. The memory of his violence was not a weight that crushed him; it was the backdrop against which grace shone.

scripture.text: But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.
scripture.understanding: One of the great sentences of grace in Scripture. “By the χάρις of God I am what I am.” His grace toward me was not κενή — empty, futile — but I κοπιάω — laboured to exhaustion — more than all of them; “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” Grace does not make you passive. It makes you work harder than anyone, and then makes you unable to take the credit.

scripture.text: Whether then it is I or they, so we preach, and so you believed.
scripture.understanding: Whether it is Paul or the other apostles, this is what they all preach, and this is what you believed. There is one gospel, not a Pauline version and a Petrine version. The resurrection is the common confession of every apostle.

scripture.text: Now if Christ is preached, that he has been raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?
scripture.understanding: The problem stated. If Christ is κηρύσσω — proclaimed — as raised from the dead, how can some among you say there is no ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν — resurrection of the dead? They likely did not deny Christ's resurrection outright; Greek thought found bodily resurrection absurd, and some may have believed in only a spiritual survival, or that the resurrection was already past (compare 2 Timothy 2:18). Paul shows that denying the general resurrection destroys Christ's resurrection too.

scripture.text: But if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ been raised.
scripture.understanding: The logic is tight. If there is no such thing as resurrection of the dead, then Christ — who was dead — has not been raised either. You cannot deny the category and keep the example.

scripture.text: If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain, and your faith also is in vain.
scripture.understanding: The first consequence. If Christ is not raised, then our κήρυγμα — preaching — is κενός, empty, and your πίστις is empty too. Christianity without the resurrection is not a weaker version of the faith. It is nothing.

scripture.text: Yes, we are also found false witnesses of God, because we testified about God that he raised up Christ, whom he didn’t raise up, if it is so that the dead are not raised.
scripture.understanding: The second consequence. The apostles are found ψευδομάρτυρες — false witnesses — of God, because they μαρτυρέω — testified — that He raised Christ. Paul is not offering an inspiring metaphor. He is making a factual claim that is either true or a lie told about God.

scripture.text: For if the dead aren’t raised, neither has Christ been raised.
scripture.understanding: The argument repeated for emphasis: if the dead are not raised, then Christ has not been raised.

scripture.text: If Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain; you are still in your sins.
scripture.understanding: The third consequence, and the most devastating. If Christ is not raised, your faith is μάταιος — futile, useless, the word used of idols — and “you are still in your sins.” The resurrection is God's public verdict that the sacrifice for sin was accepted (Romans 4:25). Without it, there is no proof that anything was paid.

scripture.text: Then they also who are fallen asleep in Christ have perished.
scripture.understanding: The fourth consequence. Those who have fallen asleep in Christ ἀπόλλυμι — have perished, are lost. Every believer who died trusting Christ would be simply gone.

scripture.text: If we have only hoped in Christ in this life, we are of all men most pitiable.
scripture.understanding: The fifth consequence. If our hope in Christ is for this life only, we are ἐλεεινότεροι — more to be pitied — than all people. Paul had given up everything for this hope: comfort, status, safety, his body. If there is no resurrection, he has been a fool, and so has every martyr.

scripture.text: But now Christ has been raised from the dead. He became the first fruits of those who are asleep.
scripture.understanding: “Νυνὶ δέ — But now!” One of the great turning points in Scripture. Christ has been raised from the dead, the ἀπαρχή — first fruits — of those who have fallen asleep. At the Feast of Firstfruits, the first sheaf of the harvest was waved before the LORD as a pledge that the whole harvest would follow (Leviticus 23:10–11). Christ's resurrection is the first sheaf. The rest of the harvest is guaranteed.

scripture.text: For since death came by man, the resurrection of the dead also came by man.
scripture.understanding: Death came δι’ ἀνθρώπου — through a man. So the resurrection came through a man. God reversed the catastrophe through the same kind of being who caused it.

scripture.text: For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.
scripture.understanding: The two Adams. In Ἀδάμ, all die — the whole human race, united to its first head, shares his death (Romans 5:12). In Christ, all will be ζωοποιέω — made alive. “All” in the second clause means all who are in Christ (v. 23 says “those who are Christ’s”). Your destiny depends on which Adam you belong to.

scripture.text: But each in his own order: Christ the first fruits, then those who are Christ’s, at his coming.
scripture.understanding: But each in his own τάγμα — order, rank; a military word for a division of troops marching in sequence. Christ the first fruits; then, ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ αὐτοῦ — at His coming — those who belong to Christ. Παρουσία was used of a king's official visit to a city. The resurrection of believers happens at the King's arrival.

scripture.text: Then the end comes, when he will deliver up the Kingdom to God, even the Father; when he will have abolished all rule and all authority and power.
scripture.understanding: Then the τέλος — the end, the goal. Christ will παραδίδωμι — hand over — the kingdom to God the Father, after He has καταργέω — rendered powerless, abolished — every ἀρχή (rule), every ἐξουσία (authority) and every δύναμις (power) opposed to God. History is not drifting. It is moving toward a handover ceremony.

scripture.text: For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet.
scripture.understanding: “He must βασιλεύω — reign — until He has put all his ἐχθροί, enemies, under his feet.” An echo of Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool.” Christ is reigning now.

scripture.text: The last enemy that will be abolished is death.
scripture.understanding: Ἔσχατος ἐχθρός — the last enemy — καταργεῖται, will be abolished: θάνατος, death. Death is not a friend, not a natural part of life to be embraced, not a door God designed. It is an enemy — the last one standing — and it has an appointment with its own destruction.

scripture.text: For, “He put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when he says, “All things are put in subjection”, it is evident that he is excepted who subjected all things to him.
scripture.understanding: Paul quotes Psalm 8:6: God “put all things in subjection under his feet.” The psalm speaks of humanity's dominion over creation; Paul applies it to Christ as the true Man who fulfils humanity's destiny. Obviously, “all things” does not include God the Father Himself, who did the subjecting.

scripture.text: When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son will also himself be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all.
scripture.understanding: When everything has been ὑποτάσσω — subjected — to the Son, then the Son Himself will be subjected to the Father, “that God may be all in all.” This is not a denial of the Son's deity; the Son is fully God. It describes His role as the Messiah who completes His mission and returns the restored kingdom to the Father, in perfect unity. The goal of history is not merely that we are saved. It is that God is all in all.

scripture.text: Or else what will they do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead aren’t raised at all, why then are they baptized for the dead?
scripture.understanding: One of the most puzzling verses in the Bible. “What will they do who are baptized ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν — for (or on behalf of) the dead?” More than forty interpretations have been proposed, and honesty requires saying we do not know exactly what the practice was. Notice that Paul says “they,” not “we” or “you”; he neither commands nor endorses it. His point is simply that the practice, whatever it was, would make no sense if the dead are not raised.

scripture.text: Why do we also stand in jeopardy every hour?
scripture.understanding: Why do we κινδυνεύω — stand in danger — every hour? Paul's whole life of risk only makes sense if the resurrection is true.

scripture.text: I affirm, by the boasting in you which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die daily.
scripture.understanding: “I die daily.” Paul swears by his καύχησις — his boasting, his pride — in them in Christ. He faced the threat of death every day. Notice: this is not mainly about spiritual self-denial, though it includes that; it is about physical danger for the gospel.

scripture.text: If I fought with animals at Ephesus for human purposes, what does it profit me? If the dead are not raised, then “let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
scripture.understanding: “If I θηριομαχέω — fought with beasts — at Ephesus.” As a Roman citizen, Paul was unlikely to have been literally thrown to animals; most interpreters take this as a vivid metaphor for savage opposition (compare Acts 19; 2 Corinthians 1:8). If there is no resurrection, what ὄφελος — gain — was it? Then he quotes Isaiah 22:13: “let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” Without the resurrection, hedonism is logical.

scripture.text: Don’t be deceived! “Evil companionships corrupt good morals.”
scripture.understanding: “Don’t be deceived!” Then a line from the Greek comic poet Menander, which had become a proverb: “Evil ὁμιλίαι — companionships, conversations — corrupt χρηστὰ ἤθη — good morals.” The people denying the resurrection were a bad influence. What you believe about the future shapes how you live now — and so does who you listen to.

scripture.text: Wake up righteously, and don’t sin, for some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.
scripture.understanding: Ἐκνήψατε — sober up, wake from a drunken stupor — δικαίως, as you ought, and stop sinning. Some have ἀγνωσία — ignorance — of God. “I say this to your shame.” A church that was proud of its knowledge is told that some of its members do not know God at all.

scripture.text: But someone will say, “How are the dead raised?” and, “With what kind of body do they come?”
scripture.understanding: Now the objection Paul expected from Greek minds: How are the dead raised? With what kind of σῶμα do they come? A Greek would imagine a rotting corpse reassembled. Paul answers the real question: what kind of body?

scripture.text: You foolish one, that which you yourself sow is not made alive unless it dies.
scripture.understanding: Ἄφρων — foolish one, mindless. The answer is in every garden. What you σπείρω — sow — is not ζωοποιέω, made alive, unless it ἀποθνῄσκω, dies. Death is not the obstacle to new life; it is the doorway to it (compare John 12:24).

scripture.text: That which you sow, you don’t sow the body that will be, but a bare grain, maybe of wheat, or of some other kind.
scripture.understanding: You do not sow the body that will be, but a γυμνὸς κόκκος — a bare, naked kernel — of σῖτος, wheat, or something else. The seed looks nothing like the plant it will become. Continuity and transformation together.

scripture.text: But God gives it a body even as it pleased him, and to each seed a body of its own.
scripture.understanding: God gives it a body as He θέλω — chose — and to each σπέρμα its own body. The same God who designs a wheat stalk from a grain can design a resurrection body from a mortal one.

scripture.text: All flesh is not the same flesh, but there is one flesh of men, another flesh of animals, another of fish, and another of birds.
scripture.understanding: Creation is full of different kinds of σάρξ — flesh: human, κτήνη (animals), ἰχθύες (fish), πτηνά (birds). God is not limited to one kind of body.

scripture.text: There are also celestial bodies, and terrestrial bodies; but the glory of the celestial differs from that of the terrestrial.
scripture.understanding: There are ἐπουράνια — heavenly bodies — and ἐπίγεια — earthly bodies — and each has its own δόξα, glory. If God can make bodies fit for the sky and bodies fit for the earth, He can make bodies fit for the age to come.

scripture.text: There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for one star differs from another star in glory.
scripture.understanding: The ἥλιος (sun), the σελήνη (moon) and the ἀστέρες (stars) each have their own glory, and star διαφέρω — differs — from star in glory. God's creativity is limitless.

scripture.text: So also is the resurrection of the dead. The body is sown perishable; it is raised imperishable.
scripture.understanding: Now four contrasts. Sown ἐν φθορᾷ — in decay, perishability — raised ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ — in imperishability, incorruption. The word “sown” is chosen deliberately: Paul speaks of burial as planting.

scripture.text: It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.
scripture.understanding: Sown ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ — in dishonour; few things are more humiliating than a corpse — raised ἐν δόξῃ, in glory. Sown ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ, in weakness; raised ἐν δυνάμει, in power. Every frailty of the body we bury will be reversed in the body we receive.

scripture.text: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body and there is also a spiritual body.
scripture.understanding: Sown a σῶμα ψυχικόν — a natural body, animated by the ψυχή, ordinary life — raised a σῶμα πνευματικόν, a spiritual body. “Spiritual” does not mean immaterial, made of spirit, a ghost. It means a body wholly governed and animated by the Holy Spirit. Jesus' risen body could be touched and could eat (Luke 24:39–43). It is more physical, not less — fully alive.

scripture.text: So also it is written, “The first man, Adam, became a living soul.” The last Adam became a life-giving spirit.
scripture.understanding: Paul quotes Genesis 2:7: the first man, Adam, became a ψυχὴ ζῶσα — a living soul, a living being. The last Adam — Christ — became a πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν — a life-giving spirit. The first Adam received life; the last Adam gives it.

scripture.text: However that which is spiritual isn’t first, but that which is natural, then that which is spiritual.
scripture.understanding: The order matters: the natural comes first, then the spiritual. We do not begin in the resurrection body; we begin in Adam's body and are transformed. Possibly a correction to some in Corinth who thought they had already attained the spiritual state.

scripture.text: The first man is of the earth, made of dust. The second man is the Lord from heaven.
scripture.understanding: The first man was ἐκ γῆς χοϊκός — from the earth, made of dust (Genesis 2:7). The second man is from οὐρανός — heaven. Christ's origin and nature are heavenly.

scripture.text: As is the one made of dust, such are those who are also made of dust; and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly.
scripture.understanding: As the dusty man, so those who are dusty; as the heavenly man, so those who are heavenly. We share the nature of the Adam we belong to.

scripture.text: As we have borne the image of those made of dust, let’s also bear the image of the heavenly.
scripture.understanding: As we have φορέω — worn, borne, as one wears clothing — the εἰκών — image — of the man of dust, so we shall (or, in some manuscripts, “let us”) bear the image of the heavenly man. The image of God, damaged in Adam, will be fully restored in Christ (Romans 8:29).

scripture.text: Now I say this, brothers, that flesh and blood can’t inherit God’s Kingdom; neither does the perishable inherit imperishable.
scripture.understanding: Σὰρξ καὶ αἷμα — flesh and blood, humanity in its present mortal condition — cannot κληρονομέω, inherit, the kingdom of God. Nor does φθορά, the perishable, inherit ἀφθαρσία, the imperishable. A transformation is necessary. Our bodies as they are now are not fit for the age to come.

scripture.text: Behold, I tell you a mystery. We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed,
scripture.understanding: Ἰδοὺ μυστήριον — behold, a mystery, something God has now revealed. Not all of us will κοιμάω — sleep, die — but all of us will be ἀλλάσσω, changed. Believers alive at Christ's return will not die; they will be transformed.

scripture.text: in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we will be changed.
scripture.understanding: Ἐν ἀτόμῳ — in an atom of time, an instant so small it cannot be cut further; the word gives us atom. Ἐν ῥιπῇ ὀφθαλμοῦ — in the flick of an eye. At the last σάλπιγξ — trumpet. For it σαλπίσει — will sound — and the dead will be raised ἄφθαρτοι, imperishable, and we will be changed. Not a slow evolution but an instantaneous transformation.

scripture.text: For this perishable body must become imperishable, and this mortal must put on immortality.
scripture.understanding: This φθαρτόν — perishable — must ἐνδύω, put on like a garment, ἀφθαρσία; this θνητόν — mortal — must put on ἀθανασία, immortality. The image is clothing: the resurrection body is put on over us, not a replacement of us.

scripture.text: But when this perishable body will have become imperishable, and this mortal will have put on immortality, then what is written will happen: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”
scripture.understanding: When that happens, the Scripture will be fulfilled: “Death is καταπίνω — swallowed up, gulped down — εἰς νῖκος, in victory” (Isaiah 25:8). The great swallower is swallowed.

scripture.text: “Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory?”
scripture.understanding: Paul bursts into a taunt song, adapted from Hosea 13:14. “Death, where is your νῖκος, victory? Hades (or Death) where is your κέντρον, sting?” The κέντρον is the sting of a scorpion or bee, or the goad used to drive cattle. Death is pictured as a beast whose stinger has been ripped out. You can still see its shape. It can no longer kill you.

scripture.text: The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.
scripture.understanding: Why did death have a sting? Because “the sting of death is ἁμαρτία, sin” — death has power over us because of sin — “and the power of sin is the νόμος, law” — the law exposes and condemns sin (Romans 7). Paul compresses the whole argument of Romans 5 to 7 into one sentence.

scripture.text: But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
scripture.understanding: Χάρις τῷ θεῷ — thanks be to God — who gives us — present tense, keeps giving — the νῖκος, the victory, through our Lord Jesus Christ. Christ dealt with sin on the cross, satisfied the law, and broke death's power in the resurrection. The victory is His, and He shares it.

scripture.text: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.
scripture.understanding: “Therefore” — the practical conclusion of the greatest theological chapter in the letter. Be ἑδραῖοι — steadfast, seated firmly — and ἀμετακίνητοι — immovable, not shifted off the hope of the gospel. Be always περισσεύω — overflowing — in the ἔργον of the Lord. Because you know that your κόπος — your labour to the point of exhaustion — is not κενός, empty, in the Lord. The resurrection guarantees that nothing done for Christ is ever wasted.

visualMeditations.title: Five Hundred Witnesses on a Hillside
visualMeditations.image: Picture a hillside in Galilee in the weeks after Passover. More than five hundred people — fishermen, farmers, women who had followed Jesus, the curious and the grieving — have gathered. And He is there. Not a ghost, not a vision in one person's head, not a rumour. He stands among them, the marks of the nails in His hands, speaking. Five hundred people see Him at the same time. Now fast-forward twenty-five years to a house in Ephesus, where Paul is dictating this letter. He writes: “most of whom remain until now.” In other words: they are still alive. Go to Galilee. Knock on their doors. Ask them what they saw.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul does not present the resurrection as a private spiritual experience or a beautiful idea. He presents it as public history with named witnesses: Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred at once, James, all the apostles, and finally Paul himself. Some were friends who had abandoned Jesus. One was a sceptical brother. One was a violent enemy. All were changed by meeting Him alive. And the creed Paul quotes — “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared” — was already being handed on within a few years of the event. Your faith rests on an empty tomb and on eyewitnesses who would not stop telling what they saw, even when it cost them their lives.

visualMeditations.title: The Seed in the Ground
visualMeditations.image: Hold a single grain of wheat in your palm. It is small, dry, hard, brown — it looks dead. Now dig a hole and bury it. Cover it with earth. Walk away. For days nothing happens, and if you dug it up you would find it softening, splitting, decaying. And then one morning a green blade breaks the surface. Weeks later it is a tall stalk, golden, heavy with grain, swaying in the wind — so different from the seed that no one who had only seen the seed could ever have imagined it. And yet it is the same life. The seed did not vanish; it was transformed.
visualMeditations.meaning: This is Paul's answer to the question, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body?” The same way a seed becomes a plant: through death into transformation. “It is sown perishable; it is raised imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body” (vv. 42–44). Notice the word “sown.” Every Christian funeral is a planting. And Jesus used the same image of His own death: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). The body you lay in the grave is the seed. The body God raises will be as different from it as the wheat stalk from the grain — and it will still be you.

visualMeditations.title: The Scorpion Without Its Sting
visualMeditations.image: Picture a scorpion — black, armoured, its tail curled high over its back, the stinger at the tip glistening with venom. Everyone in the ancient world feared it. Its sting could kill. Now picture a hand reaching down, seizing the tail, and tearing the stinger out. The scorpion still moves. It still raises its tail. It still looks frightening. But there is nothing at the end of the tail anymore. It cannot kill. And Paul stands over it and laughs: “Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory?”
visualMeditations.meaning: Death still comes to believers. We still grieve, still bury those we love, still face our own mortality. The scorpion still moves. But “the sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law” (v. 56). Death's power to destroy us came from our sin and the law's condemnation of it. And Christ took both: He bore our sin on the cross and satisfied the law's demands. Then He rose, and the stinger was gone. “But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (v. 57). Hebrews says Christ died “that through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and might deliver all of them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage” (Hebrews 2:14–15). You do not have to live in fear of a scorpion without a sting.

structure.label: The Gospel of First Importance (v. 1-11)
structure.body: Paul reminds them of the gospel they received and stand in: Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and appeared to Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred, James, all the apostles and finally to Paul — who is what he is by grace.

structure.label: If Christ Has Not Been Raised (v. 12-19)
structure.body: If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ is not raised; preaching and faith are empty, the apostles are false witnesses, believers are still in their sins, the dead in Christ have perished, and Christians are the most pitiable people on earth.

structure.label: But Now Christ Has Been Raised (v. 20-28)
structure.body: Christ is the first fruits; as in Adam all die, in Christ all will be made alive, each in order; Christ reigns until every enemy is defeated, the last being death; then He hands the kingdom to the Father, that God may be all in all.

structure.label: Living in Light of the Resurrection (v. 29-34)
structure.body: Without the resurrection, practices like baptism for the dead and Paul's daily danger make no sense, and hedonism would be logical; bad company corrupts good character — wake up and stop sinning.

structure.label: The Resurrection Body (v. 35-49)
structure.body: Like a seed that dies and is given a new body, the dead are sown perishable, dishonoured, weak and natural, and raised imperishable, glorious, powerful and spiritual; as we bore the image of the earthly Adam, we will bear the image of the heavenly.

structure.label: The Mystery and the Victory (v. 50-58)
structure.body: Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom; at the last trumpet the dead will be raised and the living changed in an instant; death will be swallowed up in victory, its sting removed through Christ — therefore be steadfast, immovable, abounding in the Lord's work.

sections.heading: The Creed, the Witnesses and the Grace That Made an Apostle
paragraphs: Chapter 15 is the longest sustained discussion of the resurrection in the Bible, and Paul saves it for the end of the letter because everything else depends on it. Some in Corinth were saying “there is no resurrection of the dead” (v. 12). They probably did not deny that something spiritual survived death; Greek philosophy widely held that the soul was immortal and the body a prison to escape. What they found absurd was the idea of a bodily resurrection — exactly the reaction of the Athenians when Paul preached the resurrection there (Acts 17:32). Paul's answer begins not with philosophy but with history and tradition: the gospel “which I preached to you, which also you received, in which you also stand, by which also you are saved” (vv. 1–2).

Verses 3 to 5 contain what most scholars, across a wide range of theological positions, recognise as an early Christian creed that Paul received and passed on. Its structure is formal and rhythmic: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures; He was buried; He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures; He appeared. Paul likely received it in Damascus or Jerusalem within a few years of his conversion — he visited Peter and James in Jerusalem three years after it (Galatians 1:18–19). That means the core Christian claims about Jesus' death and resurrection were being formulated and taught within a very short time of the events themselves. Notice also the phrase “according to the Scriptures.” The resurrection is not presented as an isolated miracle but as the fulfilment of God's long purpose revealed in Israel's Scriptures, such as Isaiah 53 and Psalm 16.

Then Paul lists the witnesses (vv. 5–8): Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred at one time, James, all the apostles, and finally Paul himself. The list functions like courtroom testimony. And Paul adds that most of the five hundred are still alive — an open invitation to check. The women who first discovered the empty tomb and saw the risen Lord, according to all four Gospels, are not mentioned, very possibly because the creed follows the form of public, legal testimony, in which a woman's witness was given little weight in that culture. And then Paul writes about himself with startling humility: “as to the child born at the wrong time… the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am” (vv. 8–10). The resurrection did not just prove a doctrine to Paul. It turned a persecutor into an apostle. Grace made him, grace drove him to work harder than anyone, and grace took the credit: “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.”

sections.heading: Everything Hangs on This: The Logic of an Empty Tomb
paragraphs: Verses 12 to 19 contain one of the most remarkable arguments in Scripture, because Paul deliberately stakes the entire Christian faith on a single historical claim. If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised (v. 13). And if Christ has not been raised, five devastating consequences follow. Our preaching is empty and your faith is empty (v. 14). The apostles are false witnesses who have lied about God (v. 15). Your faith is futile, and “you are still in your sins” (v. 17) — because the resurrection is God's public declaration that the sacrifice for sin was accepted; as Paul writes in Romans 4:25, Jesus “was raised for our justification.” Those who have died in Christ have simply perished (v. 18). And “If we have only hoped in Christ in this life, we are of all men most pitiable” (v. 19).

Many people today want a Christianity without the resurrection — a moral teacher, an inspiring example, a set of spiritual values. Paul says that such a Christianity is not a weaker version of the faith; it is no faith at all. And he is willing to say that if the resurrection did not happen, Christians are to be pitied above everyone else, because they have given up so much for a hope that is false. This is not the language of someone offering a comforting myth. It is the language of a man making a falsifiable historical claim and staking his life on it. That is why verse 32 says that without the resurrection, the logical response would be, “let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” If this life is all there is, hedonism makes sense.

“But now Christ has been raised from the dead” (v. 20). Νυνὶ δέ — the hinge on which history turns. And Paul immediately calls Christ “the first fruits of those who are asleep.” At the Feast of Firstfruits in Israel, the first sheaf of the barley harvest was waved before the LORD as an offering and a pledge that the rest of the harvest would follow (Leviticus 23:10–11). Jesus rose on the first day of the week in the Passover season — the very time when, on the most widely held reckoning, that first sheaf was offered. His resurrection is the first sheaf of a harvest that includes every believer. Then Paul sets out the two Adams: “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (v. 22). The human race is not a collection of isolated individuals. It is gathered under two heads. In Adam, death; in Christ, life. Romans 5:12–21 develops the same comparison at length.

sections.heading: The Seed, the Trumpet and the Victory
paragraphs: Verses 23 to 28 lay out the order of events. Christ rose first; then, at His coming, those who belong to Him will be raised; then comes the end, when He hands over the kingdom to the Father after destroying every hostile rule, authority and power (vv. 23–24). “For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy that will be abolished is death” (vv. 25–26). Death is not natural or friendly in Paul's theology. It is an enemy — the last one. And then a sentence that has puzzled readers: the Son Himself will be subjected to the Father, “that God may be all in all” (v. 28). This does not deny the Son's full deity; Paul has just included Him in the Shema (8:6). It describes the Messiah's completed mission: having conquered every enemy, He presents the restored creation to the Father in perfect, willing unity. The goal of history is God's glory filling everything.

Verses 29 to 34 bring the argument down to daily life. Verse 29 mentions people being “baptized for the dead,” and it must be said honestly that no one knows for certain what this practice was; more than forty explanations have been offered. Paul does not endorse it — he says “they,” not “we” — and the practice of proxy baptism developed by later groups finds no support in the rest of Scripture. Paul's only point is that the practice assumes the dead will rise. Then he points to his own life: he faces danger every hour and “dies daily” (vv. 30–31). His reference to fighting “with animals at Ephesus” (v. 32) is probably a vivid metaphor for savage opposition, since a Roman citizen would rarely be condemned to the arena. And he warns that the people denying the resurrection are corrupting the church, quoting a line from the poet Menander that had become a proverb: “Evil companionships corrupt good morals” (v. 33).

From verse 35 Paul answers the question that lay behind the denial: “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” His answer is the seed. What you sow does not come to life unless it dies, and what comes up is not the bare seed but a new body that God gives (vv. 36–38). God has made many kinds of bodies — human, animal, fish, bird, sun, moon, stars — each with its own glory (vv. 39–41). The resurrection body will be continuous with the body that is buried, yet gloriously transformed: imperishable, glorious, powerful, spiritual (vv. 42–44). “Spiritual” does not mean non-physical; Jesus' risen body could be touched and could eat (Luke 24:39–43). It means a body fully alive with the Spirit's life. And then the climax: “Behold, I tell you a mystery. We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet” (vv. 51–52). Death will be swallowed up in victory (Isaiah 25:8). Its sting, which was sin empowered by the law, has been removed through Christ (vv. 55–57). And therefore — this is where the whole great chapter lands — “be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord” (v. 58).

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: The appearances Paul lists are confirmed throughout the New Testament. The disciples in Jerusalem greeted the two from Emmaus with the news, “The Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!” (Luke 24:34) — the same appearance to Cephas that heads Paul's list. Luke says Jesus “showed himself alive after he suffered, by many proofs, appearing to them over a period of forty days” (Acts 1:3). And Jesus Himself had declared, before raising Lazarus, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies. Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?” (John 11:25–26). The risen Christ appeared to John on Patmos with the same claim in its final form: “I was dead, and behold, I am alive forever and ever. Amen. I have the keys of Death and of Hades” (Revelation 1:18).

Paul's teaching on the resurrection body is developed in his later letters. To the Romans: “if the Spirit of him who raised up Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised up Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you” (Romans 8:11), and believers groan “waiting for adoption, the redemption of our body” (Romans 8:23). To the Philippians: we wait for “the Lord Jesus Christ; who will change the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory” (Philippians 3:20–21). And to the Thessalonians, in a passage closely parallel to verses 51 and 52: “the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with God’s trumpet. The dead in Christ will rise first, then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air. So we will be with the Lord forever” (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17).

And the defeat of death, the “last enemy” of verse 26, is celebrated across the New Testament. Christ “abolished death, and brought life and immortality to light through the Good News” (2 Timothy 1:10). “Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more. Death no more has dominion over him!” (Romans 6:9). He shared our flesh and blood “that through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and might deliver all of them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage” (Hebrews 2:14–15). And the final vision of the Bible shows the last enemy gone: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain, any more. The first things have passed away” (Revelation 21:4). That is the day 1 Corinthians 15:54 looks forward to: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “a standing up again, i.e. (literally) a resurrection from death (individual, genitive case or by implication, (its author)), or (figuratively) a (moral) recovery (of spiritual truth).” The word combines ἀνά, up or again, and ἵστημι, to stand. Resurrection is not merely survival of the soul or a spiritual idea; it is a dead person standing up again in a body. That is precisely what Greek philosophy found unbelievable and what the Corinthians were tempted to deny. Paul uses the word four times in this chapter and builds the whole Christian faith on it. Jesus applied it to Himself: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). The One who stood up from the grave is Himself the standing-up of all who belong to Him.

Strong's: “a beginning of sacrifice, i.e. the (Jewish) first-fruit (figuratively).” In Israel, the first portion of the harvest was offered to God as an acknowledgement that the whole harvest was His and a pledge that the rest would follow (Leviticus 23:10–11; Exodus 23:19). The first fruits were of the same kind as the full harvest. So when Paul calls Christ “the first fruits of those who are asleep,” he is saying three things: His resurrection belongs to God; it is the beginning of a much larger harvest; and believers will be raised with the same kind of resurrection life He has. Romans 8:23 uses the same word for the Spirit as the first fruits of our future redemption. The harvest is guaranteed.

Strong's: “(properly, an adjective used as a noun) death (literally or figuratively).” Paul treats θάνατος in this chapter not as a natural process but as an enemy — “the last enemy that will be abolished” (v. 26) — that entered through Adam's sin (v. 21; Romans 5:12) and draws its power from sin and the law (v. 56). This is a strong biblical correction to the common modern idea that death is simply a natural part of life to be accepted. It is real, it is terrible, and believers grieve it. But it is defeated. Paul personifies it in verse 55 and taunts it like a conquered enemy: “Death, where is your sting?” The believer faces death not as a friend but as a defeated foe.

Strong's: “to make different.” The word describes a real transformation, not a replacement. The same verb is used in Hebrews 1:12 of the heavens and earth being changed like a garment. Paul's mystery is that believers alive when Christ returns will not die but will be changed — in an instant, “in the twinkling of an eye” — from mortal to immortal, perishable to imperishable. And the dead will be raised in the same transformed condition. The emphasis is both continuity and difference: you will still be you, but changed. Philippians 3:21 describes the same thing: Christ “will change the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory.”

Strong's: “a point (‘centre’), i.e. a sting (figuratively, poison) or goad (figuratively, divine impulse).” The word was used of a scorpion's or bee's sting (Revelation 9:10), and of the sharp goad used to drive oxen — as in Jesus' words to Saul, “It is hard for you to kick against the goads” (Acts 26:14). English “centre” comes from it, through the idea of a point. Paul pictures death as a creature with a deadly sting. And he identifies the venom: “The sting of death is sin.” Death's power to destroy comes from sin, which the law exposes and condemns. Remove the sin, and death loses its venom. That is exactly what Christ did at the cross. For the believer, death remains a creature with no sting.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with three things in this chapter: whether your faith actually rests on the resurrection, the fear of death that still holds you, and the labour you have quietly concluded is wasted.

items.title: Is Your Faith Standing on an Empty Tomb?
items.body: Paul says that if Christ is not raised, your faith is empty, you are still in your sins, and you are to be pitied. That means your Christianity is either built on the most important historical fact in the world or on nothing. The Spirit wants to ask: is your faith resting on the resurrection — or on feelings, tradition, community, or moral values that would survive just as well if Jesus had stayed in the grave? Read the list of witnesses in verses 5 to 8 slowly. Let the reality of the empty tomb settle into your bones. Your sins are forgiven because He is alive. Your future is secure because He is the first fruits. Everything you believe hangs on this. And it holds.

items.title: The Fear You Have Not Named
items.body: Hebrews says people are held in slavery all their lives by the fear of death. You may not think about it often, but it shapes more than you realise: your anxiety about health, your clinging to comfort, your terror of loss, your grief that feels hopeless, your need to control everything. The Spirit wants to name that fear and set you free from it. Death is an enemy — but it is a defeated enemy. Its sting is gone, because Christ took your sin. You will be changed, in the twinkling of an eye. The grave is a planting, not an ending. Today, speak verse 55 aloud over your fear: “Death, where is your sting?” And let the Spirit teach you to live without that chain.

items.title: Your Labour Is Not in Vain
items.body: There is something you have been doing for God that seems to bear no fruit. A prayer you have prayed for years. A child you have raised in faith who has walked away. A ministry that has not grown. Service no one notices. Faithfulness that seems to change nothing. You have quietly begun to wonder whether it is worth it. The Spirit wants you to hear the last word of this great chapter as a personal promise: “your labor is not in vain in the Lord.” Because Christ is risen, nothing done for Him is lost. Every act of faithfulness is a seed in the ground, and the harvest is guaranteed. Do not stop. Be steadfast. Be immovable. Keep abounding.

audit.title: The Foundation Check
audit.body: Write down, in your own words, why you believe Jesus rose from the dead. If your answer is mainly “because I was taught it” or “because it feels true,” spend time this week with verses 3 to 8 and the Gospel accounts (Matthew 28, Mark 16, Luke 24, John 20–21). Your faith deserves to know its foundation.

audit.title: The Fear-of-Death Check
audit.body: Ask honestly: how much does fear of death — mine or that of people I love — shape my choices, my anxieties and my priorities? Write down one area where that fear is controlling you. Then write verse 57 beside it: “But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

audit.title: The In-Vain Check
audit.body: Is there any labour for the Lord that you have stopped, or are tempted to stop, because it seems fruitless? Name it. Then ask: did I stop because God told me to, or because I lost hope? Verse 58 says your labour in the Lord is not in vain. What would it look like to pick it up again?

practices.title: Rehearsing the Creed
practices.body: Memorise verses 3 and 4 this week: “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.” Say it aloud every morning. Then, at least once this week, share it with someone — a believer who needs encouragement or an unbeliever who is curious. Tell them it is one of the oldest Christian confessions in existence, handed down within a few years of the events. Then tell them what the resurrection means to you personally.

practices.title: Planting Seeds in Hope
practices.body: Take the labour you named in the In-Vain Check. This week, do one concrete act of faithfulness in that area — pray the long prayer again, write to the child, serve in the ministry, give the gift, show up. Before you do, read verse 58 aloud. Afterward, write down the date and what you did, and title the page “Seeds Sown.” Keep adding to the page whenever you act in faith without seeing results. One day you will look back at that list in the light of the resurrection and see that none of it was wasted.

prayerReflection: “Lord Jesus, You died for my sins according to the Scriptures. You were buried. And You were raised on the third day according to the Scriptures. You appeared to Peter, to the Twelve, to more than five hundred at once, to James, to all the apostles, and to Paul — and You have made Yourself known to me. Thank You that my faith is not empty, that my sins are not still on me, that those who have died in You have not perished. You are risen indeed. Thank You that You are the first fruits, and that the harvest is guaranteed. As in Adam I die, so in You I will be made alive. Lord, I confess the fear of death that still grips me. I confess the grief that forgets hope and the anxiety that clings to this life as if it were all there is. Today I declare: death is a defeated enemy. Its sting is sin, and You took my sin. Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory? Thanks be to God, who gives me the victory through my Lord Jesus Christ. And Father, I believe that one day, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, I will be changed. This perishable will put on the imperishable. This mortal will put on immortality. Until then, make me steadfast, immovable, always abounding in Your work — because I know that my labour is not in vain in the Lord. In the mighty name of the risen Jesus, Amen.”

storyConnections.title: The Valley of Dry Bones
storyConnections.summary: The Spirit of the LORD carried Ezekiel to a valley full of bones — very many, and very dry. God asked him whether these bones could live, and Ezekiel answered that only God knew. Then God told him to prophesy to the bones. As he spoke, there was a noise and a rattling, and the bones came together, bone to bone. Sinews and flesh came on them, and skin covered them, but there was no breath in them. Then God told him to prophesy to the breath, and breath came into them, and they lived and stood up, a vast army. God said that He would open their graves and bring His people up from them, and put His Spirit in them. Ezekiel's vision was first about the restoration of Israel from exile, but it uses the language of resurrection, and it shows the God of 1 Corinthians 15: the God who gives bodies to bones and breath to the dead.

storyConnections.title: Lazarus, Come Out
storyConnections.summary: When Jesus arrived in Bethany, His friend Lazarus had been dead four days. Martha met Him and said that if He had been there, her brother would not have died. Jesus told her that her brother would rise again, and she replied that she knew he would rise in the resurrection on the last day. Then Jesus said, “I am the resurrection and the life.” At the tomb, Jesus wept. Then He told them to roll away the stone, prayed to His Father, and cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!” And the dead man came out, bound in grave clothes. Lazarus would die again one day. But his raising was a sign of the greater resurrection Jesus Himself would accomplish a few weeks later, and of the resurrection He will bring to all who believe in Him. The last enemy was put on notice in Bethany.

storyConnections.title: Abraham on Mount Moriah
storyConnections.summary: God told Abraham to take Isaac, his only son, whom he loved, and offer him as a burnt offering on a mountain in the land of Moriah. Abraham rose early, travelled three days, and climbed the mountain with Isaac carrying the wood. When Isaac asked where the lamb was, Abraham said that God would provide it. At the last moment, the angel of the LORD stopped his hand, and Abraham saw a ram caught in a thicket and offered it instead. Hebrews says that Abraham reasoned that God was able to raise Isaac even from the dead — and that, figuratively speaking, he received him back from the dead. On the third day of the journey, on that same mountain range, Abraham received his son back. Centuries later, on a hill near Jerusalem, God did not spare His own Son — and on the third day, raised Him from the dead. Abraham's faith in resurrection was answered in Christ.
